summary: Discusses security issues with the way BGP spreads routing data. BGP has no internal mechanisms to protect against attacks that modify, delete, forge, or replay data, which could disrupt routing. The document does not cover security issues with packet forwarding. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The postal system's address-sharing has no way to tell lies from truth. This memo lists how someone could cheat that system.

questions: what are the security vulnerabilities of bgp
what does tcp md5 protect in bgp
how can a bgp peer fake as path
subtitle: A walk through the ways attackers and misbehaving peers can abuse BGP routing data.

tldr.problem: BGP was designed before the Internet became hostile, and it has no internal protection against modified, deleted, forged or replayed routing data.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC goes through each BGP message type, UPDATE path attribute and supporting TCP event, and says what an outsider or a legitimate BGP peer could do with it.
tldr.outcome: It names three fundamental vulnerabilities, shows that TCP MD5 counters many outsider attacks but not bogus data from a legitimate peer, and lists possible fixes that were still controversial and not in common use.

today: RFC 4272 is an Informational RFC and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It analyses BGP as specified in RFC 4271.

sections.title: Why BGP Is Exposed
sections.content:
BGP-4 was created before the Internet became contentious, so its design includes no protection against deliberate or accidental errors. Bogus routing information can come from outsiders, who inject believable messages into a BGP session, or from true BGP peers, who can inject false routes by masquerading as another speaker or by announcing unauthorized routes as themselves. Readers are expected to know the BGP specification, RFC 4271.

The RFC lists the possible damage: starvation, congestion, blackholes, delay, looping, eavesdropping, partition, cut, churn, instability, overload, resource exhaustion and address spoofing. It does not cover security issues with forwarding packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a town where anyone can tell the mail carriers new directions and nobody checks. A prankster could send all the mail to the wrong street.

sections.title: Attacks and the Role of TCP MD5
sections.content:
The RFC checks BGP against the standard attack list. BGP carries data in cleartext and offers no replay protection. It has no protection against message insertion, deletion or modification, and because it does no peer entity authentication a man-in-the-middle attack is described as "child's play". Running over TCP makes insertion and deletion harder, since an outsider needs sequence number prediction or session stealing.

BGP implementations must support the TCP MD5 authentication mechanism. The RFC says it counters insertion, deletion, modification, man-in-the-middle and outsider denial-of-service attacks. It does not protect against eavesdropping or replay, and it cannot stop bogus data from an insider. It relies on a pre-installed shared secret, so using it must be a deliberate decision rather than a default.
sections.plainLanguage: A secret handshake between two neighbors stops strangers from butting in. It does not help if one of the neighbors lies.

sections.title: Weak Points in BGP Messages
sections.content:
The RFC finds three fundamental vulnerabilities. BGP has no internal mechanism for strong protection of message integrity, freshness and peer authenticity. It also has no way to validate an AS's authority to announce NLRI, and none to ensure the authenticity of the path attributes an AS announces.

For the four message types, a bogus OPEN, KEEPALIVE, NOTIFICATION or UPDATE sent by an outsider can disrupt the peer connection. Many errors make a speaker close the connection, delete all routes learned over it and return to Idle, which can cascade through other peers. A bogus UPDATE can also disrupt routing without breaking the connection. Peers can already close a connection at any time, so most of these cases add no extra risk from a legitimate peer.
sections.plainLanguage: A fake message can make two routers hang up on each other, and every road they told each other about disappears for a while.

sections.title: UPDATE Fields and Path Attributes
sections.content:
Forged or modified fields in an UPDATE can do real harm:

  • Withdrawn Routes: an outsider can remove legitimate routes, or replay old withdrawals.
  • AS_PATH: a malicious peer can announce a path starting with any AS, or shorten it so its route is chosen more often. That may attract traffic it would not otherwise get and can cause routing loops.
  • NEXT_HOP: a speaker can point a neighbor at a router that cannot forward the traffic, or force another AS to carry traffic it otherwise would not.
  • NLRI and originating routes: a false claim of a direct connection can make a network unreachable and can fragment aggregated address blocks.
  • ATOMIC_AGGREGATE: removing it lifts a restriction on making the NLRI more specific, so traffic may be routed incorrectly.
  • MULTI_EXIT_DISC and LOCAL_PREF: effects stay inside one AS. AGGREGATOR is not used for routing decisions, so it is no vulnerability.
sections.plainLanguage: Each part of a route announcement can be faked: who it came from, which way to go, and which street it leads to. Some fakes cause a lot more trouble than others.

sections.title: Attacks Through TCP and Supporting Protocols
sections.content:
BGP runs over TCP port 179, so it inherits TCP's weaknesses. The RFC covers SYN flooding, spoofed SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK, RST and FIN packets, and flooding of port 179, which an implementation must handle because no BGP mechanism can defeat it. TCP MD5 can counter the spoofing attacks.

BGP's security also depends secondarily on the management and configuration protocols used to signal events such as ManualStop and OpenCollisionDump, and to change timer values. If those channels are not protected, someone could tear down a BGP connection through them.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP rides inside TCP, so a trick that fools TCP also fools BGP. The tools that control the routers must be locked down too.

sections.title: Residual Risk and Operational Protections
sections.content:
TCP MD5 and IPsec do not stop attacks from a router's legitimate peers. The RFC lists four possible solutions: sign the originating AS, sign the originating AS plus predecessor information, nest signatures along the AS_PATH, or filter using a registry. It says filtering is in use near some customer attachment points but is not effective near the Internet center, and the other mechanisms are still controversial and not yet in common use.

For operations, the RFC notes that attackers can generate false traffic faster than software decryption can cope with. ISPs therefore filter packets by port number, removing traffic aimed at internal addresses and BGP port 179 at their borders. This makes denial-of-service attacks against an ISP considerably harder.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing every announcement or checking a list of allowed owners would help, but back then nobody agreed on how. Meanwhile, ISPs guard their doors with simple filters.

viz.caption: PATH ATTRIBUTES AND THEIR RISK (RFC 4272, SECTION 3.1.5.3)

items.label: Path of ASes
items.desc: Can be falsified or shortened to attract traffic or cause loops.

items.label: Border router address
items.desc: Can redirect traffic or force another AS to carry it.

items.label: IGP or EGP origin
items.desc: Small vulnerability, as it is used in route decisions.

items.label: Aggregation marker
items.desc: Removing it may cause traffic to be routed incorrectly.

items.label: Internal preference
items.desc: Affects routing within the AS only.

items.label: Last aggregator
items.desc: Not used in routing decisions, so no vulnerability.
